--- title: "Differentiation Rule: Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric Functions" aliases: - "/study/calculus/3_differentiation_rules_inverse_trigonometric.html" subtitle: "Restrict, invert, differentiate implicitly, and let the range fix the sign" date: "2026-10-24" number: "3" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: true code-fold: true theme: cosmo execute: echo: false --- An inverse trigonometric function is built in two steps: restrict a trigonometric function to an interval on which it is strictly monotone, then invert it. Every derivative in this note comes from one computation. Differentiate $f(y)=x$ implicitly to get $dy/dx = 1/f'(y)$, then rewrite $f'(y)$ in terms of $x$ with a Pythagorean identity. The identity determines $f'(y)$ only up to sign, and **the range of the inverse function fixes the sign**. That single observation explains every formula, every excluded point, and every convention dispute below. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Trig function on ℝ
(not one-to-one)"] --> B["Restrict to a
monotone interval"] B --> C["Inverse function
range = that interval"] C --> D["f(y) = x
differentiate implicitly"] T["Inverse function theorem"] --> D D --> E["dy/dx = 1 / f′(y)"] E --> F["Pythagorean identity
sign fixed by the range"] F --> G["Derivative formulas"] ``` # Defining the Inverse Functions ## Why a restriction is needed A function has an inverse exactly when it is one-to-one. Sine, cosine and tangent are periodic, so each value is attained infinitely often and no inverse exists on the full domain. The remedy is to restrict each function to an interval on which it is strictly monotone and still attains every value of its range. The standard (principal) choices are: | Function | Restricted to | Inverse | Domain of inverse | Range of inverse | |---|---|---|---|---| | $\sin x$ | $[-\pi/2,\ \pi/2]$ | $\sin^{-1}x = \arcsin x$ | $[-1,1]$ | $[-\pi/2,\ \pi/2]$ | | $\cos x$ | $[0,\ \pi]$ | $\cos^{-1}x = \arccos x$ | $[-1,1]$ | $[0,\ \pi]$ | | $\tan x$ | $(-\pi/2,\ \pi/2)$ | $\tan^{-1}x = \arctan x$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $(-\pi/2,\ \pi/2)$ | Each inverse is defined by an equivalence that states the range condition explicitly: $$ \begin{aligned} \sin^{-1}x = y &\iff \sin y = x \ \text{ and } \ -\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le y\le\tfrac{\pi}{2},\\ \cos^{-1}x = y &\iff \cos y = x \ \text{ and } \ 0\le y\le\pi,\\ \tan^{-1}x = y &\iff \tan y = x \ \text{ and } \ -\tfrac{\pi}{2}< y<\tfrac{\pi}{2}. \end{aligned} $$ The range condition is not decoration. It is exactly the information that the equation $\sin y = x$ alone does not contain, and every sign decision below comes from it. The notation $\sin^{-1}x$ means the inverse function, not $(\sin x)^{-1} = \csc x$. Graphically, the inverse is the reflection of the restricted graph across the line $y=x$ (@fig-inverses). ::: {#cell-fig-inverses .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Each inverse (blue) is the reflection of the restricted function (gray) across $y=x$. The vertical asymptotes $x=\pm\pi/2$ of the restricted tangent become the horizontal asymptotes $y=\pm\pi/2$ of $\tan^{-1}$.](3_differentiation_rules_inverse_trigonometric_files/figure-html/fig-inverses-output-1.png){#fig-inverses width=1048 height=345} ::: ::: ## Cancellation equations The two compositions behave differently: $$ \sin(\sin^{-1}x) = x \quad (-1\le x\le 1), \qquad \sin^{-1}(\sin x) = x \quad \left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right). $$ The first holds on the whole domain of $\sin^{-1}$. The second holds only on the restricted interval: for any real $x$, $\sin^{-1}(\sin x)$ is the unique angle in $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ with the same sine as $x$. For example, $$ \sin^{-1}\!\left(\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \tfrac{\pi}{4}, \qquad \sin^{-1}(\sin\pi) = 0 . $$ Over all of $\mathbb{R}$, the map $x\mapsto \sin^{-1}(\sin x)$ is a triangle wave of period $2\pi$ that agrees with $x$ only on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ (@fig-sawtooth). The same pattern holds for cosine on $[0,\pi]$ and tangent on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$. ::: {#cell-fig-sawtooth .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: $\sin^{-1}(\sin x)$ is a triangle wave that equals $x$ only on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$. Right: its derivative is $\mathrm{sgn}(\cos x)$, derived in the chain-rule examples.](3_differentiation_rules_inverse_trigonometric_files/figure-html/fig-sawtooth-output-1.png){#fig-sawtooth width=950 height=326} ::: ::: ## Continuity A strictly monotone function on an interval whose image is an interval has no jumps, because a jump would leave a gap in the image. Each inverse above is strictly monotone and its image is the restriction interval, so $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$ are continuous on their domains. Continuity is the hinge of the differentiability proof below. # Derivative of an Inverse Function ## Implicit differentiation Let $y = f^{-1}(x)$, so $f(y) = x$. Assuming $f^{-1}$ is differentiable, differentiate both sides with respect to $x$: $$ f'(y)\,\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{f'(y)}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad (f^{-1})'(x) = \frac{1}{f'\big(f^{-1}(x)\big)} . $$ ## Geometric reading Reflection across $y=x$ sends a point $(a,b)$ to $(b,a)$, so it sends a tangent direction $(1,m)$ to $(m,1)$. The slope becomes $1/m$: rise and run swap roles. In particular, a horizontal tangent of $f$ ($m=0$) becomes a vertical tangent of $f^{-1}$. ## Inverse function theorem (one variable) The computation above assumed that $f^{-1}$ is differentiable. The following theorem removes that assumption. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Theorem"} Let $f$ be continuous and strictly monotone on an interval $I$, and let $y_0\in I$. If $f$ is differentiable at $y_0$ and $f'(y_0)\neq 0$, then $f^{-1}$ is differentiable at $x_0 = f(y_0)$ and $$ (f^{-1})'(x_0) = \frac{1}{f'(y_0)} . $$ ::: *Proof.* For $x\neq x_0$ in $f(I)$, put $y = f^{-1}(x)$. Injectivity gives $y\neq y_0$, so the difference quotient can be inverted: $$ \frac{f^{-1}(x) - f^{-1}(x_0)}{x - x_0} = \frac{y - y_0}{f(y) - f(y_0)} = \left[\frac{f(y) - f(y_0)}{y - y_0}\right]^{-1}. $$ As $x\to x_0$, continuity of $f^{-1}$ gives $y\to y_0$ with $y\neq y_0$, so the bracket tends to $f'(y_0)\neq0$ and the quotient tends to $1/f'(y_0)$. If $y_0$ is an endpoint of $I$, the same argument gives a one-sided derivative. $\blacksquare$ The step "$x\to x_0$ implies $y\to y_0$" is exactly where continuity of the inverse enters. Implicit differentiation uses it silently. ## When $f'(y_0) = 0$: vertical tangents If $f'(y_0) = 0$, then $f^{-1}$ is **not** differentiable at $x_0$. Were it differentiable, the chain rule applied to $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ would give $$ f'(y_0)\,(f^{-1})'(x_0) = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0 = 1 . $$ The identity in the proof says more. The difference quotient of $f^{-1}$ is the reciprocal of a quantity tending to $0$. For increasing $f$ that quantity is positive, so the quotient tends to $+\infty$ and the graph of $f^{-1}$ has a vertical tangent at $x_0$. # Inverse Sine Let $y = \sin^{-1}x$, so $\sin y = x$ with $-\pi/2\le y\le\pi/2$. Implicit differentiation gives $$ \cos y\,\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\cos y}. $$ The Pythagorean identity gives only $\cos y = \pm\sqrt{1-\sin^2 y} = \pm\sqrt{1-x^2}$. On the range $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$, $\cos y\ge 0$, so the sign is $+$: $$ \boxed{\ \frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}, \qquad -1M$, monotonicity gives $$ \frac{\pi}{2}-\varepsilon = \tan^{-1}M < \tan^{-1}x < \frac{\pi}{2}. $$ The case $x\to-\infty$ follows because $\tan^{-1}$ is odd. **Example.** With $t = 1/(x-2)$, we have $t\to\infty$ as $x\to2^+$ and $t\to-\infty$ as $x\to2^-$, so $$ \lim_{x\to2^+}\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x-2} = \frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad \lim_{x\to2^-}\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x-2} = -\frac{\pi}{2}. $$ The function has a jump of size $\pi$ at $x = 2$, so no value at $x=2$ can make it continuous. # Simplifying Compositions ## Method To evaluate $g(h^{-1}(x))$ for trigonometric $g$ and $h$: set $\theta = h^{-1}(x)$, read off $h(\theta) = x$, use a Pythagorean identity to obtain $g(\theta)$ up to sign, and fix the sign from the range of $h^{-1}$. A right-triangle sketch reproduces the magnitude, but by itself it only covers $\theta>0$. The range argument covers every $x$. **Example.** For $\theta = \tan^{-1}x$, $\sec^2\theta = 1+\tan^2\theta = 1+x^2$. Since $\sec\theta>0$ on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, $$ \cos(\tan^{-1}x) = \frac{1}{\sec\theta} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}. $$ **Example.** For $\theta = \sin^{-1}\frac13$, the range gives $\cos\theta = +\sqrt{1-\frac19} = \frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$, so $$ \tan\left(\sin^{-1}\tfrac13\right) = \frac{1/3}{2\sqrt2/3} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}. $$ ## Table of compositions | | $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$ | $\theta=\cos^{-1}x$ | $\theta=\tan^{-1}x$ | |---|---|---|---| | $\sin\theta$ | $x$ | $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ | $\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$ | | $\cos\theta$ | $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ | $x$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$ | | $\tan\theta$ | $\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ $(\lvert x\rvert<1)$ | $\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}$ $(x\neq0)$ | $x$ | Every bare square root sits exactly where the range forces $\sin\theta\ge0$ or $\cos\theta\ge0$. Wherever the sign can vary, it is carried by the factor $x$. # The Remaining Three Inverses ## Inverse cotangent Restrict $\cot$ to $(0,\pi)$. Then $\cot^{-1}:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\pi)$, and from $\cot y = x$, $$ -\csc^2y\,\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{d}{dx}\cot^{-1}x = -\frac{1}{1+\cot^2y} = -\frac{1}{1+x^2}. $$ Equivalently $\cot^{-1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}-\tan^{-1}x$, proved exactly like the arcsine-arccosine identity: with $\theta=\tan^{-1}x$, we have $\pi/2-\theta\in(0,\pi)$ and $\cot(\pi/2-\theta) = \tan\theta = x$. ## Inverse secant: two conventions $\sec^{-1}$ is defined for $|x|\ge1$, and here the restriction interval is genuinely a choice. Two conventions are in common use: $$ \text{(A)}\ \ y\in\left[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\cup\left[\pi,\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right), \qquad \text{(B)}\ \ y\in\left[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\cup\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\pi\right]. $$ In both, the branch for $x\ge1$ lies in $[0,\pi/2)$. They differ in where the branch for $x\le-1$ lives. From $\sec y = x$, $$ \sec y\tan y\,\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{x\tan y}, \qquad \tan^2y = \sec^2y - 1 = x^2-1 . $$ The sign of $\tan y$ is the whole story. **Convention (A).** The $x\le-1$ branch lies in the third quadrant, where $\tan y\ge0$. Hence $\tan y = \sqrt{x^2-1}$ on both branches and $$ \frac{d}{dx}\sec^{-1}x = \frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^2-1}}, \qquad |x|>1 . $$ **Convention (B).** The $x\le-1$ branch lies in the second quadrant, where $\tan y\le0$. Hence $\tan y = \operatorname{sgn}(x)\sqrt{x^2-1}$ and $$ \frac{d}{dx}\sec^{-1}x = \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}, \qquad |x|>1 . $$ **Trade-off.** Convention (A) gives a derivative with no absolute value, which is convenient when the formula is read backward as an antiderivative. Convention (B) gives the identity $\sec^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}(1/x)$ and a function that is increasing on each branch. Under (A), the $x\le-1$ branch is $\sec^{-1}x = 2\pi - \cos^{-1}(1/x)$, which is decreasing; this is why $1/(x\sqrt{x^2-1})$ is negative there. ## Inverse cosecant The structure is identical. From $\csc y = x$ we get $-\csc y\cot y\,y' = 1$, so $y' = -1/(x\cot y)$ with $\cot^2y = x^2-1$. - Convention (A), $y\in(0,\pi/2]\cup(\pi,3\pi/2]$: $\cot y\ge0$ on both branches, so $\frac{d}{dx}\csc^{-1}x = -\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^2-1}}$. - Convention (B), $y\in[-\pi/2,0)\cup(0,\pi/2]$: $\cot y$ has the sign of $x$, so $\frac{d}{dx}\csc^{-1}x = -\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}$. # Chain Rule Examples ## A composite with a corner Let $f(x) = \sin^{-1}(x^2-1)$. **Domain.** $-1\le x^2-1\le1 \iff 0\le x^2\le2 \iff |x|\le\sqrt2$, so the domain is $[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]$. **Derivative.** The outer derivative requires $|x^2-1|<1$, that is $00$, the product and chain rules give $$ f'(x) = \tan^{-1}\sqrt x + x\cdot\frac{1}{1+x}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt x} = \tan^{-1}\sqrt x + \frac{\sqrt x}{2(1+x)} . $$ At $x=0$ the chain rule does not apply, since $\sqrt x$ is not differentiable there, but the definition does: $\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x} = \tan^{-1}\sqrt x\to0$ as $x\to0^+$. So $f'(0)=0$ as a right-hand derivative, matching the limit of the formula. ## The triangle wave For $\cos x\neq0$, $$ \frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}(\sin x) = \frac{\cos x}{\sqrt{1-\sin^2x}} = \frac{\cos x}{|\cos x|} = \operatorname{sgn}(\cos x). $$ The slope is $\pm1$ and switches at odd multiples of $\pi/2$, which is exactly the triangle wave of @fig-sawtooth. Writing $\sqrt{1-\sin^2x} = \cos x$ would wrongly give slope $1$ everywhere. # Rigor Notes ## Zero derivative does not imply constant Let $g(x) = \tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}(1/x)$ for $x\neq0$. Then $$ g'(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2} + \frac{1}{1+x^{-2}}\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{x^2}\right) = \frac{1}{1+x^2} - \frac{1}{x^2+1} = 0 . $$ Yet $g(1) = \pi/2$ and $g(-1) = -\pi/2$. The mean value theorem forces $g$ to be constant only on each interval of its domain, and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ consists of two intervals. Hence $g(x) = \frac{\pi}{2}\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ (@fig-arctan-sum). ::: {#cell-fig-arctan-sum .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![$\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}(1/x)$ has zero derivative on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ but takes the value $\pi/2$ for $x>0$ and $-\pi/2$ for $x<0$.](3_differentiation_rules_inverse_trigonometric_files/figure-html/fig-arctan-sum-output-1.png){#fig-arctan-sum width=662 height=355} ::: ::: ## Where each hypothesis is used - **Strict monotonicity on an interval:** existence of the inverse, and its continuity. - **Continuity of the inverse:** the implication $x\to x_0 \Rightarrow y\to y_0$ in the proof of the theorem. - **$f'(y_0)\neq0$:** differentiability of the inverse. Its failure produces the vertical tangents of $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$ at $x=\pm1$. - **The range:** the sign of every square root. ## Reading the formulas backward The derivatives are algebraic functions while the inverse trigonometric functions are not. Read backward, the formulas give antiderivatives of algebraic functions that leave the algebraic world: $$ \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \sin^{-1}x + C, \qquad \int\frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \tan^{-1}x + C . $$ # Summary | Function | Domain | Range | Derivative | Valid for | |---|---|---|---|---| | $\sin^{-1}x$ | $[-1,1]$ | $[-\pi/2,\ \pi/2]$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ | $\lvert x\rvert<1$ | | $\cos^{-1}x$ | $[-1,1]$ | $[0,\ \pi]$ | $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ | $\lvert x\rvert<1$ | | $\tan^{-1}x$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $(-\pi/2,\ \pi/2)$ | $\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ | $x\in\mathbb{R}$ | | $\cot^{-1}x$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $(0,\ \pi)$ | $-\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ | $x\in\mathbb{R}$ | | $\sec^{-1}x$ (A) | $\lvert x\rvert\ge1$ | $[0,\pi/2)\cup[\pi,3\pi/2)$ | $\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ | $\lvert x\rvert>1$ | | $\sec^{-1}x$ (B) | $\lvert x\rvert\ge1$ | $[0,\pi/2)\cup(\pi/2,\pi]$ | $\frac{1}{\lvert x\rvert\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ | $\lvert x\rvert>1$ | | $\csc^{-1}x$ (A) | $\lvert x\rvert\ge1$ | $(0,\pi/2]\cup(\pi,3\pi/2]$ | $-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ | $\lvert x\rvert>1$ | | $\csc^{-1}x$ (B) | $\lvert x\rvert\ge1$ | $[-\pi/2,0)\cup(0,\pi/2]$ | $-\frac{1}{\lvert x\rvert\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ | $\lvert x\rvert>1$ | **Common pitfalls** - $\sin^{-1}x$ is not $1/\sin x$. - $\sin^{-1}(\sin x) = x$ only for $x\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$. - $\sqrt{1-\sin^2y}=|\cos y|$. Dropping the absolute value is legitimate only when the range guarantees $\cos y\ge0$. - The derivative formulas fail at $x=\pm1$: vertical tangents for $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$, and the same for $\sec^{-1}$ and $\csc^{-1}$. - Before using a $\sec^{-1}$ or $\csc^{-1}$ formula, check which range convention is in force.
